questions.prompt: What is the key difference between data management and data governance, as this course defines them?
options: Data management is the day-to-day operational work of handling data; data governance is the decisions, roles, and rules that determine how that work should happen
Data management and data governance are two names for the same activity
Data governance is only performed by external regulators, never by employees
Data management only applies to Salesforce, while data governance applies to every other system
questions.explain: Management is the operational work (entering, updating, reporting on data); governance is the upstream layer of roles, policy, and process that determines how that work is supposed to happen.
questions.distractorExplain: Treating them as the same activity misses the point of Lesson 1: a Salesforce admin deduplicating a batch of Accounts is doing management, while deciding that duplicates should be blocked at the point of entry -- and who owns that decision -- is governance.

questions.prompt: A sales rep owns (via OwnerId) a hundred Account records in Salesforce. Her manager asks her to also act as the Account object's governance-level data owner. Per this course, what is the main problem with that request?
options: There is no problem; record ownership and data ownership are the same authority

Record ownership is a security/access mechanism over individual records, while data ownership requires org-wide authority over standards and dispute resolution -- a different scope than owning records day to day
Salesforce technically prevents any user from being both a record owner and a data owner
Only Salesforce admins are allowed to be data owners
questions.explain: Lesson 2 draws this distinction directly: owning records through OwnerId/OWD/role hierarchy is a different scope of authority than being accountable for an object's data standards and definitions across the whole org.

questions.prompt: Match each stewardship role to the task it's responsible for, per Lesson 3.
right: Decides what values belong in a picklist and reviews duplicate-record reports for business accuracy
Configures the Matching Rule and Duplicate Rule settings that implement the business decision
Manages Shield Platform Encryption keys and org-wide backup/recovery
Resolves which department's definition of a field should win when two teams disagree
questions.explain: The business steward owns functional quality decisions, the technical steward (admin) implements them in configuration, the custodian handles infrastructure-level controls, and the data owner has the standards-setting and dispute-resolution authority above all three.

questions.prompt: An org wants duplicate Leads to be automatically prevented. What does this course say is required for that to actually happen in Salesforce?
options: Nothing -- Salesforce blocks duplicate Leads automatically out of the box
A Matching Rule defining how duplicates are detected, plus an activated Duplicate Rule referencing it with a Block (or Alert/Report) action -- none of this is on by default
Only a Validation Rule is needed; Matching and Duplicate Rules are unrelated to deduplication
Duplicate prevention can only be achieved through a third-party AppExchange package
questions.explain: Lesson 4 corrects the common misconception that Salesforce blocks duplicates by default -- Matching Rules and Duplicate Rules exist as standard features but must be deliberately activated and configured.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Duplicate Rule's action can be set to Alert, Report, or ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 4 describes the three Duplicate Rule actions as Alert (warn the user), Report (log for later review without interrupting), and Block (prevent the save outright).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about data-quality metrics, per Lesson 5.
options: A completeness rate measures the percentage of records with no blank value in a defined set of required fields
A duplication rate should realistically target 0% for every object
A Duplicate Rule's Report action can be used purely as a measurement tool without disrupting daily record creation
Accuracy is best measured through a sampled manual audit against a trusted external reference, since Salesforce can't verify real-world correctness automatically
Data-quality metrics only need to be reported once, since the underlying data never changes
questions.explain: Completeness rate and the Report-action measurement technique are both described directly in Lesson 5, as is the sampled-audit approach to accuracy. A 0% duplication target is specifically called unrealistic, and metrics need a recurring review cadence, not a one-time report.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 5 recommend a declining-trend target like "below 3% and falling" for duplication rate, instead of a flat 0% target?
options: Because duplication rate cannot be measured at all in Salesforce
Because fuzzy matching has real limits and new data sources keep introducing fresh risk, so reaching 0% would require Block rules so aggressive that legitimate new records get rejected
Because 0% duplication is always trivially achievable with no tradeoffs
Because Duplicate Rules are deprecated and no longer apply to any object
questions.explain: The lesson explains that driving duplication to zero would require overly aggressive blocking that harms legitimate record creation, so a realistic program targets a declining trend instead of an unachievable hard zero.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 6, what does a real data retention policy cover?
options: Only the exact date a record must be deleted
The record's full lifecycle -- how long it's actively used, whether and when it's archived, and only then when it's finally deleted
Only which fields on the record are required
Only whether the record was created via the UI or the API
questions.explain: Lesson 6 defines retention as a lifecycle policy spanning active use, archiving, and eventual deletion -- not a single deletion deadline.
questions.distractorExplain: Reducing retention to just a deletion date skips the harder middle question the lesson raises: a record no longer needed day-to-day often still has to be kept, in some form, for a defined period before deletion is even allowed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce's native Compliance Categorization field commonly includes options such as PII, HIPAA, CCPA, and ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 lists GDPR alongside PII, HIPAA, CCPA, and PCI as commonly-seeded Compliance Categorization options that identify which regulation makes a given field relevant.

questions.prompt: Match each privacy/consent concept to its correct description, per Lesson 7.
right: Default is 'no' processing until an affirmative legal basis is established
Default is 'yes' collection/sale until the individual actively exercises a right to stop it
Revoking a specific permission previously given; if it was the only legal basis, processing generally must stop
A narrower, often temporary request to pause active use of data without necessarily withdrawing consent or deleting it
questions.explain: GDPR's opt-in and CCPA's opt-out are opposite defaults; consent withdrawal revokes a legal basis entirely, while restriction of processing is a narrower, often temporary pause -- the two are related but not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: A company deletes a customer's primary Contact record in response to a GDPR erasure request and considers the request complete. Per Lesson 8, what has likely been missed?
options: Nothing -- deleting the Contact record is always sufficient on its own

Related records (Cases, Opportunities, custom-object children) may still reference the person, and the data may have already propagated to downstream systems like a marketing platform or backup snapshot that Salesforce deletion doesn't reach
Erasure requests under GDPR do not apply to Contact records
The Recycle Bin automatically notifies every connected system when a record is deleted
questions.explain: Lesson 8 stresses that a real erasure process has to account for related records and for every downstream system the data was synced to, since deletion inside Salesforce doesn't automatically reach those other places.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Salesforce's native field-level classification metadata, per Lesson 9.
options: Data Sensitivity Level, Compliance Categorization, Data Owner, and Field Usage are four separate metadata attributes that can be set per field
Tagging a field as Restricted automatically triggers Shield Platform Encryption on that field
These classification fields are manually-applied metadata tags, not an automated content scan
An org can customize its own Data Sensitivity Level and Compliance Categorization picklist values through Data Classification Settings
Classification only delivers real value once something downstream, like an encryption rollout or access review, actually reads and acts on the labels
questions.explain: The four metadata attributes are real and customizable, and they are tags a human applies rather than an automatic scan or enforcement mechanism -- tagging a field Restricted does not, by itself, change any Salesforce behavior like triggering encryption.

questions.prompt: A regulator asks which user exported a large number of sensitive Contact records without changing any of them. Per Lesson 10, which native/Shield feature is specifically built to answer this kind of question?
options: Setup Audit Trail, since it tracks all data activity
Field History Tracking, since it logs every record view
Event Monitoring (Shield), since it captures usage events like exports, logins, and API calls -- not just changes
The Individual object, since it stores consent preferences
questions.explain: Lesson 10 distinguishes change-tracking features (Setup Audit Trail, Field History) from usage-tracking: viewing or exporting records without changing them is only visible through Event Monitoring.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a Salesforce record's retention lifecycle in the order Lesson 6 describes them.
items: The record is actively created and used in daily operations
The record (or its field history) is archived into a lower-cost, less immediately accessible store
The record passes through the Recycle Bin's short recovery window after deletion is initiated
questions.explain: Lesson 6 frames retention as a full lifecycle: active use, then archiving (which still costs storage and isn't the same as deletion), then an initiated deletion passing through the Recycle Bin's short recovery window, and finally permanent removal.

questions.prompt: A new custom field holding health data goes live with no one checking whether it needs a Data Sensitivity Level. Per Lesson 11, what kind of framework gap does this reveal?
options: A data-quality gap unrelated to the governance framework
A missing release-strategy checkpoint -- the framework's change process has no point where a new field is reviewed against classification/retention requirements before it ships
Proof that data classification is not a real Salesforce feature
A problem that only Shield licensing can fix, unrelated to process
questions.explain: Lesson 11 argues a framework that's silent on how changes reach production creates exactly this hole -- new risk enters right where no data-governance checkpoint exists in the release process.

questions.prompt: Match each type of change to the review tier Lesson 12's tiered change process assigns it to.
left: A typo fix in a picklist label
A new field added to an already-governed object, affecting two teams
A Data Cloud rollout unifying customer data across three orgs
An urgent production bug fix with no data-governance impact
right: Individual sub-team, no committee involvement needed
Routine monthly batch review with a lightweight governance checklist item
Major change requiring its own dedicated, full governance review
Expedited individual handling outside the routine batch cycle
questions.explain: Lesson 12's tiered model matches review effort to actual risk: trivial fixes need no committee review, routine multi-team changes get a lightweight checklist in a batch review, and major changes like a Data Cloud rollout get a full dedicated review; urgent low-impact fixes still get handled promptly outside the routine cycle.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a well-formed Salesforce governance committee, per Lesson 12.
options: A committee staffed only by the admin team will systematically under-weight business risk it doesn't have visibility into
A committee that personally reviews every single change, no matter how small, avoids becoming a bottleneck
A well-formed committee commonly includes representation from IT/the platform team, business operations, and legal/compliance or security
The escalation path to the committee should define who can bring an issue, how often it meets, and how decisions get recorded
Governance committees should never resolve disputes between departments -- that's solely the data owner's job
questions.explain: An IT-only committee misses business risk, and a well-formed one draws from multiple functions with a clearly defined escalation path. Reviewing every change regardless of size is exactly the bottleneck the tiered process exists to prevent, and the committee is specifically where cross-department disputes the data owner can't resolve alone get escalated.

questions.prompt: In the Meridian Health Partners case study (Lesson 13), put these response steps in the correct order once the erasure request and audit finding both surface in the same week.
items: Identify every place the patient's data lives, including the unmaintained third-party integration
Resolve the erasure request across Salesforce and the downstream system in parallel with the audit response
Classify Treatment_Notes__c with a Data Sensitivity Level and Compliance Categorization
Use the new classification to decide on encryption, extended audit retention, and access-review scope
Fix the structural gaps: name a Contact data owner and add a classification checkpoint to the release process
questions.explain: The case study treats the immediate response (finding all copies of the data, resolving the request, classifying the field, and acting on that classification) as happening first and in parallel, with the structural fix -- naming an owner and adding a release-process checkpoint -- as the follow-up step that prevents recurrence.

questions.prompt: A governance program reports "we held 12 committee meetings this year" as evidence of success. Per Lesson 14, what's missing from this claim?
options: Nothing -- meeting count is the best available measure of governance success
An outcome metric -- the report doesn't say whether anything actually improved, like a falling duplication rate or a shrinking time-to-resolve for erasure requests
The names of every committee member who attended
Proof that Salesforce Shield was purchased
questions.explain: Lesson 14 distinguishes activity metrics (easy to count, always trend upward) from outcome metrics (harder to produce, but the only ones that prove something actually got better).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 1, the four pillars a governance program rests on are people, policy, process, and ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 names people, policy, process, and technology as the four pillars -- a program missing any one of them fails in a predictable way, such as policy without process going stale.
